metadata.scope: e_caspian-pontic_steppe (all baronies across k_caspian_steppe, k_caucasus, k_pontic_steppe, k_qara_dala, and x_script_5503)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_basagha.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym in the Caspian steppe.
b_basagha.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh compound from bas ('head, main') and agha ('elder brother, senior'), used as a clan or personal name and later steppe toponym; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_temir.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1870 CE (with nearby Temir fortification/fair established 1870–1879 CE) on the Temir River in Aktobe Region.
b_temir.etymology_analysis: Named after the Temir River (from Turkic/Kazakh temir, 'iron'), a tributary of the Emba; the modern town was founded in 1870 CE.

b_ak_su.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented for this West Kazakhstan steppe settlement/hydronym.
b_ak_su.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh hydronym Aqsu (aq 'white, clear' + su 'water, river'), referring to clear steppe streams; settlements bearing this name in West Kazakhstan and Aktobe regions are modern and unattested by 867 CE.

b_jaksybai.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Zhaksybai in 1992 CE (previously Sverdlovo); the Zhaksybai River and personal/clan name are unattested in pre-867 CE sources.
b_jaksybai.eponym_details: Named after the Kazakh personal/clan name or river Zhaksybai (lit. 'good rich man / noble').
b_jaksybai.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Jaqsybai (jaqsy 'good' + bai 'wealthy man, lord'), a traditional Kazakh anthroponym and local hydronym in West Kazakhstan; the modern village took the name in 1992 CE, with no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_isanbai.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; Turkic/Kazakh anthroponymic toponym (comparable to Bashkir Isanbayevo attested 1707 CE).
b_isanbai.eponym_details: Derived from the Turkic personal name Isanbai / Esenbai ('healthy/well + rich man').
b_isanbai.etymology_analysis: Turkic personal name compound Isanbai/Esenbai (isen/esen 'healthy, safe' + bai 'lord, wealthy man'), applied to steppe tracts and settlements; no attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_manatau.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic toponym and Zhagalbaily clan name.
b_manatau.eponym_details: Associated with the Kazakh personal/clan name Manatau (Zhagalbaily genealogy of West Kazakhstan/Orenburg).
b_manatau.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh oronym and clan name ending in tau ('mountain, hill'); attested in modern Kazakh genealogy and steppe toponymy, with no pre-867 CE written record.

b_kyz_imchik.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; modern Kazakh/Turkic oronym (e.g., Mount Kyzemshek in West Kazakhstan Region).
b_kyz_imchik.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic descriptive oronym Qyzemshek ('maiden's breast'), applied to twin-peaked hills across the Kazakh steppe including Shyngyrlau District in West Kazakhstan; unattested in pre-867 CE sources.

b_jambalar.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; Turkic steppe toponym.
b_jambalar.etymology_analysis: Turkic pluralized toponym in -lar, likely from a Kipchak/Kazakh clan or personal name; no historical attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_yalachi.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; Turkic steppe toponym.
b_yalachi.etymology_analysis: Turkic agentive noun in -chi; unattested in pre-867 CE historical records.

b_maza.first_mention_attestation: Settlement founded in 1580 CE (named after the Maza River in Samara Oblast).
b_maza.etymology_analysis: Named after the Maza River in the Middle Volga region (from Mordvin mazi 'beautiful' / maza 'shallow', or Tatar maza 'calm'); the settlement formed in 1580 CE.

b_maloi_irghiz.first_mention_attestation: Documented in 1763 CE in the Russian Imperial Manifesto Register of Available Land along the Volga ('Maly Irgiz River').
b_maloi_irghiz.etymology_analysis: Russian-Turkic hybrid hydronym combining Russian maloi ('lesser') with the Turkic river name Irgiz (Yrghyz); the Russian-qualified form is post-867 CE.

b_pecheneg.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the latter half of the 8th century CE (c. 750–800 CE) as Be-ča-nag in a Tibetan/Uyghur diplomatic report; later in Regino of Prüm (889 CE) and Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (10th century CE).
b_pecheneg.etymology_analysis: Turkic ethnonym (Bäčänäk / Bečenek) for the nomadic confederation inhabiting the Volga-Ural steppe in the 8th–9th centuries CE, attested in an 8th-century Tibetan/Uyghur report and 9th–10th century Byzantine/Latin chronicles.

b_ilekskoi_gorodok.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1737 CE by Yaik Cossacks (named Ileksky Gorodok on 1 July 1737 CE).
b_ilekskoi_gorodok.etymology_analysis: Russian-Turkic name meaning 'fortified town on the Ilek', combining the Turkic hydronym Ilek (from ilek/elik 'roe deer') with Russian gorodok ('small town/fort'); founded in 1737 CE.

b_kamelik.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in 1859 CE in the Lists of Populated Places of the Russian Empire (Samara Governorate); the Kamelik hydronym has no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_kamelik.etymology_analysis: Hydronym in Saratov and Samara Oblasts, derived either from Bashkir kämälek ('river of boats', kämä + -lek) or an Indo-Iranian root kem ('water'); not attested in pre-867 CE sources.

b_zhaltyr.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; modern Kazakh/Turkic hydronym and settlement name.
b_zhaltyr.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym Zhaltyr ('shining, glittering'), referring to open, treeless, mirror-like steppe lakes in West Kazakhstan; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kalmikovsky.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 1730s–1740s CE as Kalmykovskaya Fortress on the Ural (Yaik) River.
b_kalmikovsky.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival form from the ethnonym Kalmyk (Oirat Mongols who migrated to the Volga-Ural steppe in the 17th century CE); the fortress was built in the 1730s–1740s CE.

b_yaitsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1584 CE as Yaitsky Gorodok (modern Oral/Uralsk, renamed Uralsk in 1775 CE).
b_yaitsk.etymology_analysis: Russian town name Yaitsk / Yaitsky Gorodok derived from the Yaik (Ural) River (Turkic Jayıq, related to Ptolemy's 2nd-century CE Daïx); the Cossack settlement was founded in 1584 CE.

older_name_by_867.notes: The Ural/Yaik River itself is attested in Ptolemy (2nd century CE) as Daïx, but the settlement of Yaitsk was founded in 1584 CE (nearby Golden Horde Zhayyk dates to the 13th century CE).

b_tasqala.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented for the settlement (formerly Russian Kamenskaya, renamed Tasqala).
b_tasqala.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Tasqala ('stone fortress/town'), a calque of its earlier Russian name Kamenskaya; modern settlement with no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_tserlona.first_mention_attestation: Earliest traditional founding date 1567 CE (other historical records cite 1711 or 1725 CE) as the Greben/Terek Cossack stanitsa of Chervlyonaya.
b_tserlona.etymology_analysis: Russian Cossack stanitsa name Chervlyonaya ('crimson/red'), transferred from Chervlyony Yar in the Ryazan region; founded no earlier than 1567 CE.

b_cisterki.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; unattested CK3 barony name in Ciscaucasia.
b_cisterki.etymology_analysis: Unattested toponym in Ciscaucasia; no historical record of this name exists on or before 867 CE.

b_derbent.first_mention_attestation: Founded/fortified as a Sasanian Persian fortress (Darband) in 438 CE (earlier known as Albana/Chor; Arabic Bab al-Abwab from the 7th–8th century CE).
b_derbent.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Darband ('closed/barred gate'), referring to the Sasanian fortification built in 438 CE across the narrow Caspian coastal pass.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE, as Albana, a coastal city of Caucasian Albania) and early Armenian/Byzantine sources (5th–6th century CE as Chor / Čor / Tzour, preceding Sasanian Darband in 438 CE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Albana (c. 150 CE) and Armenian/Byzantine Chor / Tzour preceded the Sasanian Persian fortress name Darband (Derbent, 438 CE).

b_kumukh.first_mention_attestation: First reliable historical attestation dates to the 6th century CE under the Sasanian Empire; conquered by the Umayyad Caliphate in 734 CE with a mosque built in 778 CE.
b_kumukh.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Lak toponym (Ghumuq / Kumukh), attested from the 6th century CE as the political and cultural center of the Lak people in Dagestan.

b_balanjar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 630s–650s CE as the capital of the Baranjar/Khazar state and site of the 652 CE Arab-Khazar Battle of Balanjar.
b_balanjar.eponym_details: Legendary founder Balanjar ibn Yafith mentioned by later medieval chroniclers Ibn al-Faqih and Abu al-Fida.
b_balanjar.etymology_analysis: Early medieval Khazar/Baranjar city name attested in 7th–8th century CE Arabic and Caucasus sources, serving as the first Khazar capital until the 720s CE.

b_kuba.first_mention_attestation: Earliest attestation of the name Qubat/Cuba in the 11th century CE ('Bade-Firuz Qubat') and 12th-century CE Arabic sources.
b_kuba.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 11th–12th century CE (Bade-Firuz Qubat, Arabic Cuba/Kubba); originated from the village of Gudial and became seat of the Quba Khanate in the 18th century CE.

b_samander.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zabender in Theophylact Simocatta (c. 598 CE) and as Samandar in 8th-century CE Arabic accounts of the Khazar capital (720s–750s CE).
b_samander.etymology_analysis: Either from Middle Persian ('farthest gate') or the Hunnic tribal name Zabender (attested c. 598 CE); served as the second Khazar capital in the 720s–750s CE.

b_durdzukia.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 7th century CE as Dourtsk (Դուրծկք) in Anania Shirakatsi's Geography of Armenia and in medieval Georgian chronicles.
b_durdzukia.eponym_details: Linked in later Georgian chronicle tradition to a legendary eponymous ancestor Durdzuk.
b_durdzukia.etymology_analysis: Latinized choronym from the medieval Georgian and Armenian exonym Durdzuk/Dourtsk for the Vainakh peoples of the North Caucasus, attested from the 7th century CE.

b_sambalut.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern scholarship reconstructs Transcaucasian 'sam-' toponyms as Khazar-era foundations, without a dated primary-source attestation.
b_sambalut.etymology_analysis: Khazar-era Caucasian town name containing the Khazar prefix sam- ('high, top, main'), associated with 7th–8th century CE Khazar rule in the Caucasus.

b_samiran.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern scholarship reconstructs Transcaucasian 'sam-' toponyms as Khazar-era foundations, without a dated primary-source attestation.
b_samiran.etymology_analysis: Khazar-era Caucasian town name with the Khazar prefix sam- ('high, top, main'), associated with 7th–8th century CE Khazar presence in the Caucasus.

b_kizlyar.first_mention_attestation: First documented reference in 1609 CE; Russian fortress founded in 1735 CE.

morphemes.translation: girls (or red cliff/branch of the Terek)

b_kizlyar.etymology_analysis: From Turkic/Kumyk Qızlar (literally 'girls', or associated with a Terek River branch meaning 'red cliff'); first documented in 1609 CE.

older_name_by_867.notes: Some historians associate the Kizlyar area with medieval Samandar, which is already a separate barony (b_samander) in e_caspian-pontic_steppe.

b_cabartei.first_mention_attestation: Identified as a distinct political entity by the 1440s CE in the Arabic chronicle al-Uqud al-Jawhariyya; Kabardian expansion dates to the 14th–15th centuries CE.
b_cabartei.etymology_analysis: Choronym Kabardey (variant Cabartei), denoting the Eastern Circassian principality that emerged in the Central/North Caucasus in the 1440s CE.

b_azov.first_mention_attestation: 1067 CE (Kipchak conquest, renamed Azaq; later Golden Horde Azak and Venetian/Genoese Tana in the 13th century CE)
b_azov.etymology_analysis: From Kipchak Turkic Azaq ('lowland' or 'river mouth'), applied after the 1067 CE Kipchak conquest and later adapted into Russian Azov.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Bosporan Greek inscriptions, archaeological evidence (first quarter of the 3rd century BCE, c. 275 BCE), and Strabo's Geography.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek emporion of Tanais stood in the Don delta nearby before its 3rd-century CE destruction.

b_manych.first_mention_attestation: 17th century CE (early modern Russian cartography and Cossack records; anciently called Lik / Lycus)
b_manych.etymology_analysis: From the Manych River (West/East Manych in the Kuma-Manych Depression), derived from Turkic manach ('bitter/brackish', referring to its saline lakes); anciently known as Lik.

b_chamchev.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; appears to be a game-coined or corrupted Russian-style surname toponym in the Azov delta
b_chamchev.etymology_analysis: Unattested historical toponym; structurally resembles a Russian possessive/surname-derived settlement name ending in -ev.

b_yergolyk.first_mention_attestation: Late 18th century CE (Russian imperial surveys of the North Caucasus steppe)
b_yergolyk.etymology_analysis: Variant of Yegorlyk (Bolshoy Yegorlyk River), from Turkic ägri ('curved') + -lyk, later folk-etymologized in Russian under the influence of the personal name Yegor.

b_yaseni.first_mention_attestation: 1873 CE (stanitsa Yasenskaya founded near the Yaseni River; khutor Yaseni in Starominsky District originally Russkaya Koloniya)
b_yaseni.etymology_analysis: Russian plural yaseni ('ash trees'), referring to the Yaseni River and coastal spit on the Sea of Azov in Kuban.

b_chelbaska.first_mention_attestation: 1885 CE (stanitsa Chelbasskaya founded on the Sredny Chelbas River; Chelbas postal station attested in 19th-century Kuban)
b_chelbaska.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival form from the Chelbas River (likely Turkic/Nogai chelbas, 'shallow water' or 'steppe river').

b_tikhon.first_mention_attestation: 1874 CE (Tikhoretsk railway station / Tikhon'kiy settlement on the Tikhon'kaya River in Kuban)

morphemes.translation: quiet, calm (or personal name Tikhon from Greek Tychon)

b_tikhon.etymology_analysis: In the Kuban context near Chelbaska, corresponds to the Tikhon'kiy / Tikhoretsk area on the Tikhon'kaya ('quiet') River, though the bare form Tikhon also matches the Slavicized Greek personal name Tychon.

b_tmutarakan.first_mention_attestation: c. 950 CE (Byzantine Greek Tamatarcha in Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus's De Administrando Imperio; Old East Slavic Tmutarakan in the 11th century CE)
b_tmutarakan.etymology_analysis: Old East Slavic Tъmutorokanь, adapted from Byzantine Greek Tamatarcha / Khazar Tamantarkhan (possibly from Adyghe tamə + t'arqʷo, 'branching wing', describing the Taman Peninsula).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 6th century BCE (ancient Greek colony of Hermonassa founded by Mytilene on the Taman Peninsula)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek colony of Hermonassa preceded medieval Tamatarcha/Tmutarakan on the exact same site.

b_papagia.first_mention_attestation: c. 950 CE (attested as Παπαγία in Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus's De Administrando Imperio as a region beyond Zichia)
b_papagia.etymology_analysis: Recorded in Byzantine Greek as Papagia (Παπαγία) in De Administrando Imperio (c. 950 CE) for a polity in the northwestern Caucasus beyond Zichia.

b_kuban.first_mention_attestation: 14th century CE (Turkic/Kipchak hydronym Qoban / Kuban; anciently attested as Greek Hypanis in the 5th century BCE)
b_kuban.etymology_analysis: From the Kuban River, whose Turkic name Qoban ('rising/overflowing') replaced the ancient Greek Hypanis and medieval Circassian Psyzh.

b_soleny.first_mention_attestation: 20th century CE (modern settlement of Solyony in Temryuksky District, Krasnodar Krai, on the Taman Peninsula)
b_soleny.etymology_analysis: Russian adjective solyony ('salty'), naming a settlement near saline lakes/estuaries on the Taman Peninsula.

b_atkarsk.first_mention_attestation: 1780 CE (sloboda Etkara renamed Atkarsk and granted town status; predecessor Tatar settlement at the mouth of the Atkara River)
b_atkarsk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Atkara (Etkara) River at its confluence with the Medveditsa, with the Russian town-forming suffix -sk added in 1780 CE.

b_peschanka.first_mention_attestation: 19th century CE (rural settlement of Peschanka in Atkarsky District, Saratov Oblast, on the Peschanka River)
b_peschanka.etymology_analysis: Russian hydronymic formation from pesok ('sand') + -anka, referring to the sandy-bedded Peschanka River.

b_tersa.first_mention_attestation: 18th century CE (Russian settlement and hydronymic records along the Tersa River, a tributary of the Medveditsa)
b_tersa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tersa River (a right tributary of the Medveditsa in Saratov and Volgograd oblasts); the hydronym is likely of Turkic or steppe substrate origin.

b_penza.first_mention_attestation: 1663 CE (founded as a Russian frontier fortress on the Penza and Sura rivers)

morphemes.translation: end of a swampy river / border

b_penza.etymology_analysis: Named after the Penza River, whose hydronym derives from Moksha Mordvinic penza ('end of a swampy river' or 'boundary').

b_saransk.first_mention_attestation: 1641 CE (founded as the Russian frontier fortress of Saransk at the confluence of the Saranka and Insar rivers)
b_saransk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Saranka River (from Mordvinic sara, 'swampy/sedge-covered river') with the Russian urban suffix -nsk.

b_insara.first_mention_attestation: 1647 CE (Insar fortress built on the Insar / Inzara River along the southeastern Russian defensive line)
b_insara.etymology_analysis: From the Insar (Moksha: Inzara) River, a Mordvinic hydronym meaning 'great/wide marshy river'.

b_chechkeiev.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; appears to be a game-coined or corrupted Mordvinic/Tatar-Russian surname toponym in the Penza region
b_chechkeiev.etymology_analysis: Unattested historical toponym; structurally a Russian possessive/surname-style formation (-ev) on a Mordvinic or Turkic stem.

b_petrovsk.first_mention_attestation: 1698 CE (founded by personal decree of Tsar Peter the Great to defend the Saratov frontier)
b_petrovsk.eponym_details: Peter the Great (Pyotr I of Russia, 1672–1725), who ordered the fortress built in 1698 CE.
b_petrovsk.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive town name Petr-ov-sk, 'city of Peter', named after Tsar Peter the Great upon its 1698 CE foundation.

b_treliaka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; appears to be a game-coined or corrupted toponym in the Petrovsk/Saratov region
b_treliaka.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or modern Russian gazetteers; likely a game-coined or garbled regional name.

b_alchanka.first_mention_attestation: 1724 CE (settlement of Alshanka / Bolshaya Olshanka in Saratov Oblast first mentioned)
b_alchanka.etymology_analysis: Variant of Alshanka / Olshanka, a Russian hydronym and settlement name derived from olkha ('alder') referring to alder-lined streams.

b_saratov.first_mention_attestation: 1590 CE (founded as a Russian fortress on the Volga near the ruined Golden Horde city of Ukek)
b_saratov.etymology_analysis: Russified from Turkic Sary-tau ('Yellow Mountain', referring to Sokolova Gora); stands near the 13th–14th century Golden Horde city of Ukek (Uvek).

b_hanbalik.first_mention_attestation: 1264–1271 CE (Mongol-Turkic Khanbaliq, 'City of the Khan', originally the Yuan capital in Beijing; misplaced in CK3 as a Volga steppe barony)
b_hanbalik.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Mongolic compound Khan-balyq ('City of the Khan'), historically the Yuan capital (Beijing) and used here as a generic Turko-Mongol steppe city name.

b_uza.first_mention_attestation: 18th century CE (Russian hydrographic records of the Uza River, left tributary of the Sura in Penza and Saratov oblasts)
b_uza.etymology_analysis: Named after the Uza River (a left tributary of the Sura in Penza and Saratov oblasts), a pre-Russian Finno-Ugric or Turkic hydronym.

b_kerkinitis.first_mention_attestation: c. 500 BCE (ancient Greek colony of Kerkinitis / Κερκινίτις founded on the western Crimean coast)
b_kerkinitis.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Κερκινίτις (Kerkinitis), attested from c. 500 BCE on the site of modern Yevpatoria (later Khazar Güzliev and Crimean Tatar Kezlev).

b_kalos_limen.first_mention_attestation: 4th century BCE (ancient Greek colony of Kalos Limen / Καλός Λιμήν in northwestern Crimea, attested in the Periplus of the Euxine Sea)
b_kalos_limen.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Καλός Λιμήν (Kalos Limen, 'Beautiful/Charming Harbor'), founded by Greek colonists in the 4th century BCE near modern Chornomorske.

b_kerch.first_mention_attestation: 1068 CE (Old East Slavic Korchev / Кърчевъ on the Tmutarakan Stone; Italian Cerchio in the 13th–14th centuries CE)
b_kerch.etymology_analysis: Modern Kerch derives from Old East Slavic Korchev (11th century CE), replacing earlier Greek Panticapaeum and Byzantine Bosporus.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Late 7th–6th century BCE (Milesian Greek colony of Pantikapaion, later Byzantine Bosporus)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded as Pantikapaion (Panticapaeum) c. 600 BCE; known as Bosporus in late antiquity and early Byzantine times.

b_chersonesus.first_mention_attestation: 6th century BCE (ancient Greek colony of Chersonesos / Χερσόνησος founded by settlers from Heraclea Pontica; later Byzantine Cherson)
b_chersonesus.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Χερσόνησος (Chersonesos, 'peninsula', literally 'land-island'), founded in the 6th century BCE on the outskirts of modern Sevastopol.

b_theodosia.first_mention_attestation: 6th century BCE (ancient Greek colony of Theodosia / Θεοδοσία founded by colonists from Miletus)
b_theodosia.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Θεοδοσία (Theodosia, 'God-given'), founded in the 6th century BCE by Milesian Greeks; later medieval Caffa / Kefe and modern Feodosia.

b_aqmescit.first_mention_attestation: c. 1500 CE (Crimean Tatar town of Aqmescit, residence of the Qalğa-Sultan in the Crimean Khanate)
b_aqmescit.etymology_analysis: Crimean Tatar Aqmescit ('White Mosque' or 'Western Mosque'), founded in the Crimean Khanate era and incorporated into Simferopol in 1784 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 3rd century BCE (royal capital of the Crimean Scythians, Greek Neapolis / Νεάπολις, within modern Simferopol)
older_name_by_867.notes: Scythian Neapolis flourished from the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE at the same river crossing of the Salhir.

b_perekop.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (East Slavic Perekop, translating Crimean Tatar Or Qapı and ancient Greek Taphros)
b_perekop.etymology_analysis: East Slavic Perekop ('dug-across'), a calque of the ancient Greek Taphros ('trench') describing the defensive ditch across the Crimean isthmus.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 1st century BCE – 2nd century CE (Greek Taphros / Τάφρος attested in Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek Taphros ('trench') was the classical name for the fortified ditch and settlement on the Perekop Isthmus.

b_dzhankoi.first_mention_attestation: 1855 CE (first documented mention of the Crimean Tatar village of Dzhankoi / Canköy)
b_dzhankoi.etymology_analysis: From Crimean Tatar Canköy (< cañı köy, 'new village'; alternatively can köy, 'spirit village', or linked to the Circassian Zhaney tribe).

b_golden_hills.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; English rendering of a generic steppe topographic name ('Golden Hills' / Zolotye Gory / Altyn-Tau) in the Don valley
b_golden_hills.etymology_analysis: English translation of a descriptive oronymic name ('Golden Hills') used in Crusader Kings III for a county/barony in the Don valley.

b_siyahtepe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement; Turkic descriptive oronym Siyah-tepe ('Black Hill') used as a steppe barony in the Don valley
b_siyahtepe.etymology_analysis: Turkic compound siyah ('black', from Persian) + tepe ('hill, kurgan'), an unattested descriptive hill name in the Don valley.

b_ust-donvokhi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; appears to be a game-coined/corrupted Russian river-mouth name ('Ust-Don...')
b_ust-donvokhi.etymology_analysis: Compound beginning with Russian ust- ('river mouth') and Don, followed by an unattested/corrupted element -vokhi.

b_kazarki.first_mention_attestation: Modern archaeological site designation (Kazarki, a 7th–10th century CE Khazar settlement north of Sarkel); contemporary 867 CE name is unattested
b_kazarki.etymology_analysis: Modern Russian designation for a Khazar-era archaeological settlement north of Sarkel, derived from the ethnonym Khazar (or Russian kazarka, 'brent goose').

b_kazanskaya.first_mention_attestation: 1647 CE (Don Cossack stanitsa of Kazanskaya founded on the Don River in Rostov Oblast)
b_kazanskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival stanitsa name Kazanskaya, associated with the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God or settlers from the Kazan region.

b_boguchar.first_mention_attestation: 1704 CE (founded as a Cossack settlement on the Boguchar / Bouchar River; earlier nearby settlement shown on Isaac Massa's 1638 map)
b_boguchar.etymology_analysis: Named after the Boguchar (earlier Bouchar / Bogucharka) River, a tributary of the Don; the hydronym's exact origin is uncertain.

b_millerovo.first_mention_attestation: 1786 CE (founded as a khutor on the estate of military starshina Ivan Miller on the Glubokaya River)
b_millerovo.eponym_details: Ivan Abramovich Miller, a Don Cossack military starshina of German descent granted the land in 1786 CE.
b_millerovo.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive settlement name Miller-ovo ('Miller's estate'), named after its 1786 CE founder Ivan Miller.

b_podgornye.first_mention_attestation: 19th century CE (common Russian rural settlement name Podgornoye / Podgorny in the Don basin)
b_podgornye.etymology_analysis: Russian locational adjective podgornye ('below/at the foot of the hills'), a descriptive settlement name rather than a bare natural feature.

b_sarysyn.first_mention_attestation: 1589 CE (Russian fortress of Tsaritsyn founded on the Volga, adapted from Turkic Sary-su / Sarychin)
b_sarysyn.etymology_analysis: From Turkic Sary-su ('yellow/muddy water', referring to the Tsaritsa River) or Sary-chin ('yellow island'), later folk-etymologized in Russian as Tsaritsyn (modern Volgograd).

b_frolovo.first_mention_attestation: 1859 CE (first written mention of the Don Cossack khutor of Frolov in the List of Inhabited Places of the Don Host Oblast)
b_frolovo.eponym_details: Frolov, the Cossack founder/eponym of khutor Frolov (from the Russian personal name Frol, < Latin Florus).
b_frolovo.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive settlement name Frol-ovo ('Frolov's khutor'), first attested in 1859 CE.

b_kamyshin.first_mention_attestation: 1667 CE (founded on the left bank of the Kamyshinka River; relocated to Dmitriyevsk in 1710 CE and renamed Kamyshin in 1780 CE)
b_kamyshin.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kamyshinka River, from Russian kamysh ('reed', borrowed from Turkic qamyş) + -in.

b_yelan.first_mention_attestation: 1691 CE charter of Peter I granting lands along the Tersa and Yelan rivers to boyar Lev Naryshkin.
b_yelan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Russian dialectal topographic term yelan' ('extensive glade or meadow plain', borrowed from Turkic alan/yalan), also borne by the Yelan River; settled in the late 17th century CE.

b_balachev.first_mention_attestation: 17th-century CE foundation of Balashovo khutor by yasak peasant Grigory Bolashev; granted town status as Balashov in 1780 CE.
b_balachev.eponym_details: Named after Grigory Bolashev, a 17th-century CE yasak peasant who founded the original khutor on the Khopyor River.
b_balachev.etymology_analysis: Possessive Russian toponym formed from the surname of its 17th-century CE founder, Grigory Bolashev (ultimately from Turkic balash, 'child').

b_khoper.first_mention_attestation: 1389 CE Russian chronicle account (Journey of Metropolitan Pimen) mentioning the Khopyor (Khoper) River.
b_khoper.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Khopyor River, the largest left tributary of the Don; first attested in Russian sources in 1389 CE, with no documented attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_viazovka.first_mention_attestation: 1700 CE foundation of the village of Vyazovka in Saratov Oblast.
b_viazovka.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name derived from vyaz ('elm') with the toponymic suffix -ovka, after the local Vyazovka stream; founded in 1700 CE.

b_khopyor.first_mention_attestation: 1389 CE Russian chronicle account (Journey of Metropolitan Pimen) mentioning the Khopyor River.
b_khopyor.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic title referring to the Khopyor River, first attested in 1389 CE; unattested in surviving written sources on or before 867 CE.

b_bychok.first_mention_attestation: 1724 CE church register of Voronezh Governorate (settled c. 1718–1720 CE).

morphemes.translation: promontory or hillock at a river confluence

b_bychok.etymology_analysis: From the Old Russian dialectal topographic term bychok denoting a hillock or promontory at the confluence of two rivers (here the Bychok and Tolucheyevka); settled c. 1718–1720 CE.

b_kriucha.first_mention_attestation: Early 19th-century CE foundation of Kriusha (formerly Krivusha) on the Ikorets River (uninhabited in 1780 CE).
b_kriucha.etymology_analysis: Originally Krivusha (later Kriusha, rendered in-game as Kriucha), named after a sharp bend in the river channel; founded in the early 19th century CE.

b_manina.first_mention_attestation: 1743–1748 CE foundation of Manina sloboda by Ukrainian Cossacks of the Ostrogozhsk Regiment.

morphemes.translation: personal name or local river root

b_manina.etymology_analysis: East Slavic possessive settlement name (sloboda Manina, modern Manino) established in the 1740s CE along the Manina River.

b_tuluchezeva.first_mention_attestation: 1716 CE foundation of the Cossack settlement of Tulucheyevka (Tolucheyevo) in Voronezh Oblast.
b_tuluchezeva.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation (Tolucheyevo / Tulucheyevka, rendered in-game as Tuluchezeva) of the Turkic hydronym Tulu-chay ('full river'); settled in 1716 CE.

b_lejlotka.first_mention_attestation: No documented historical attestation found for 'Lejlotka' (likely a garbled or modern local Khopyor-basin toponym).
b_lejlotka.etymology_analysis: Obscure toponym in the Khopyor-Tolucheyevka basin with no attested pre-867 CE form or verified etymology.

b_trotskhoper.first_mention_attestation: 1774 CE records of Pugachev's Rebellion mentioning Trostyanka on the Khopyor River near Balashov.
b_trotskhoper.etymology_analysis: Compound rendering of Trostyanka-on-the-Khopyor (from Russian trost' 'reed' and the Khopyor River), a village in Balashov District attested in the late 18th century CE.

b_cherkassy.first_mention_attestation: 1286 CE traditional foundation/first mention of Cherkasy (celebrated 725th anniversary in 2011 CE).
b_cherkassy.etymology_analysis: Derived from the East Slavic ethnonym Cherkasy (originally referring to Circassians or steppe Cossack groups); first attested in the late 13th century CE.

b_sacacatce.first_mention_attestation: No documented historical attestation found for 'Sacacatce' in the Middle Dnieper / Cherkasy region.
b_sacacatce.etymology_analysis: Unidentified holding name in the Cherkasy county with no verified pre-867 CE attestation or documented etymology.

b_kashan.first_mention_attestation: No documented historical attestation found for 'Kashan' in the Cherkasy / Southern Bug region.
b_kashan.etymology_analysis: Unidentified holding name in the Cherkasy county with no verified pre-867 CE attestation in the Pontic steppe.

b_pervomaisk.first_mention_attestation: 1919 CE merger of Olviopol (founded 1676 CE), Bohopil, and Holta (1762 CE) under the Soviet name Pervomaisk.
b_pervomaisk.etymology_analysis: Soviet-era commemorative name coined in 1919 CE from pervomay ('May Day', 1 May); the earliest predecessor settlement at the confluence (Orlyk/Olviopol) dates to 1676 CE.

b_kherson.first_mention_attestation: 18 June 1778 CE decree of Catherine the Great founding Kherson on the lower Dnieper.
b_kherson.etymology_analysis: Named in 1778 CE under Catherine the Great's 'Greek Project' after the ancient Crimean colony of Chersonesus (Greek Khersónēsos, 'peninsula').

b_kazanka.first_mention_attestation: 1800 CE foundation of Kazanka in Mykolaiv Oblast by settlers from Kursk Governorate.

morphemes.translation: Kazan (Icon of the Mother of God)

b_kazanka.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1800 CE and named after the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God, a post-867 CE Russian Orthodox devotion.

b_voznessensk.first_mention_attestation: 1795 CE imperial Russian foundation of Voznesensk on the site of the 18th-century CE Cossack settlement of Sokoly.
b_voznessensk.etymology_analysis: Imperial Russian toponym from 1795 CE named in honor of the Feast of the Ascension (Vozneseniye), replacing the earlier Cossack settlement of Sokoly.

b_beryslav.first_mention_attestation: 1784 CE Russian renaming of the 15th-century CE Ottoman fortress Kazikermen as Beryslav.
b_beryslav.etymology_analysis: Slavicized imperial name ('take glory') bestowed in 1784 CE upon the former Lithuanian customs post (late 14th century CE) and Ottoman fortress of Kazikermen.

b_nikopol.first_mention_attestation: 1782 CE Russian imperial renaming of Mykytyn Rih (attested 16th–17th century CE) as Nikopol.
b_nikopol.etymology_analysis: Classicalizing name ('City of Victory', Greek Nikopolis) given in 1782 CE to the former Zaporozhian Cossack crossing and Sich at Mykytyn Rih.

b_okachiv.first_mention_attestation: 1492 CE construction of Kara-Kerman / Özü fortress by Meñli I Giray; later Ottoman Achi-Kale / Ochakiv.
b_okachiv.etymology_analysis: East Slavic adaptation of the 15th–16th century CE Crimean Tatar and Ottoman fortress name (Kara-Kerman / Özü / Achi-Kale), built near the ancient Greek colony of Alektor.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Dio Chrysostom, Borystheniticus (Oration 36), c. 95 CE (colony founded 7th–6th century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek colony of Alektor (Ἀλέκτωρ) stood on or immediately adjacent to the site of Ochakiv.

b_tiraspol.first_mention_attestation: 1792 CE foundation of Tiraspol by Russian generalissimo Alexander Suvorov.
b_tiraspol.etymology_analysis: Neo-classical compound ('City on the Tyras/Dniester') coined at its 1792 CE Russian foundation.

b_odessa.first_mention_attestation: 1794 CE decree of Catherine the Great establishing Odessa on the site of Khadjibey (1529 CE) / Kotsiubijiv (1415 CE).

morphemes.translation: adaptation of classical Pontic city name

b_odessa.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1794 CE by Catherine the Great and named after the ancient Greek colony of Odessos (originally Varna, mistakenly placed here in 18th-century antiquarianism).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian, Periplus Ponti Euxini, c. 131 CE (Greek settlement from 6th century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Greek settlement from the 6th century BCE located at modern Odesa, attested as the Port of the Istrians (Istrianon Limen).

b_olbia_ETEL.first_mention_attestation: 7th century BCE (c. 647 BCE) Milesian Greek foundation; attested in Herodotus (Histories, Book IV, c. 450 BCE) as Olbia.
b_olbia_ETEL.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek colony (Olbia Pontike) founded in the 7th century BCE by Milesian colonists on the Southern Bug (Hypanis) estuary; clearly attested long before 867 CE.

b_bakhmut.first_mention_attestation: 1571 CE mention of Bakhmut as a Russian border guard post on the Bakhmutka River.

morphemes.translation: stream/river name (possibly from personal name Mahmut or Turkic horse term)

b_bakhmut.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bakhmut (Bakhmutka) River, a tributary of the Seversky Donets; the settlement originated as a 16th-century CE frontier post (1571 CE).

b_tor.first_mention_attestation: 1645 CE construction of the Tor fortress (Torsky Ostrog) at the salt lakes (renamed Sloviansk in 1784 CE).
b_tor.etymology_analysis: Historical name (until 1784 CE) of Sloviansk, taken from the Tor (Kazennyi Torets) River; the fortress was founded in 1645 CE.

b_volcha.first_mention_attestation: Vovcha (Volcha) River in Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts; no documented attestation on or before 867 CE.
b_volcha.etymology_analysis: East Slavic hydronym ('Wolf River', Ukrainian Vovcha, Russian Volchya), a major tributary of the Samara River; unattested in sources <= 867 CE.

b_lozova.first_mention_attestation: 1869 CE foundation of Lozova railway station in Kharkiv Oblast.
b_lozova.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lozova River (from Ukrainian loza 'willow/vine'); the modern city was founded as a railway station in 1869 CE.

b_pokrovsk.first_mention_attestation: 1875 CE establishment of Grishino railway station (renamed Krasnoarmiisk in 1938 CE and Pokrovsk in 2016 CE).
b_pokrovsk.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1875 CE as Grishino railway station and renamed Pokrovsk in 2016 CE after the Orthodox feast of Pokrova (Intercession).

b_samar.first_mention_attestation: 1576 CE charter of Polish King Stephen Báthory mentioning the town of Samara (Old Samar).
b_samar.etymology_analysis: Named after the Samara River (a left tributary of the Dnieper); the Cossack town of Samar is first attested in 1576 CE (renamed Novomoskovsk in 1794 CE, restored to Samar in 2024 CE).

b_karlivka.first_mention_attestation: 1670s CE settlement of Orchyk; renamed Karlivka in the 18th century CE.
b_karlivka.eponym_details: Named in the 18th century CE after a post-867 CE noble owner named Karl (replacing the earlier 1670s CE settlement name Orchyk / Minikhpol).
b_karlivka.etymology_analysis: Ukrainian possessive settlement name formed from the personal name Karl, replacing the 1670s CE Cossack settlement of Orchyk.

b_kharka.first_mention_attestation: 1654 CE foundation of Kharkiv (Kharka) in Sloboda Ukraine.
b_kharka.etymology_analysis: Variant rendering of Kharkiv (founded 1654 CE), named after the Kharkiv River (though folk tradition links it to a 17th-century CE Cossack named Kharko).

b_bohodukhiv.first_mention_attestation: 1662 CE foundation of Bogodukhov ostrog by Ukrainian Cossacks under Otaman Tymofiy Krysa.
b_bohodukhiv.etymology_analysis: Ukrainian Christian toponym meaning 'of the Spirit of God' (Boho-dukh-iv), founded as a Cossack sloboda and fort in 1662 CE.

b_cheboksary.first_mention_attestation: 1469 CE Russian chronicle mention of Cheboksary (preceded by 13th-century CE Volga Bulgarian Veda Suvar).
b_cheboksary.etymology_analysis: First attested in Russian chronicles in 1469 CE, likely adapted from the Turkic name Çabaqsar (local Chuvash name Šupaškar); archaeological predecessor Veda Suvar dates to the 13th century CE.

b_urmary.first_mention_attestation: 1775 CE administrative census of Kazan Governorate listing the village of Malyye Urmary.
b_urmary.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of Chuvash Vărmar ('forest, woodland', cf. Turkic orman), first attested in 1775 CE as Malyye Urmary.

b_tzyvil.first_mention_attestation: 1584 CE (or 1589 CE) Muscovite foundation of Tsivilsk at the confluence of the Bolshoy and Maly Tsivil rivers.
b_tzyvil.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tsivil River (Chuvash Săval, 'stream/overflow'); the Muscovite fortress of Tsivilsk was founded in 1584–1589 CE.

b_alatyr.first_mention_attestation: 1552 CE foundation of the Muscovite fortress of Alatyr at the confluence of the Sura and Alatyr rivers.
b_alatyr.etymology_analysis: Named after the Alatyr River (a tributary of the Sura); founded as a Russian fortified outpost in 1552 CE on the site of an earlier Mordvin village.

b_lachyk-uba.first_mention_attestation: No documented historical attestation found for 'Lachyk-Uba' on or before 867 CE.
b_lachyk-uba.etymology_analysis: Turkic compound toponym (lachyk + uba 'mound/camp') in the Mordvinia-Tambov steppe borderland, unattested in sources <= 867 CE.

b_morchansk.first_mention_attestation: 1623 CE first mention of the village of Morsha (granted town status as Morshansk in 1779 CE).
b_morchansk.etymology_analysis: Formed in 1779 CE from the earlier village name Morsha (first attested 1623 CE) with the Russian town suffix -nsk.

b_rakcha.first_mention_attestation: 1678 CE cadastre (pistsovaya kniga) of Prince V. V. Kropotkin mentioning the village of Raksha.
b_rakcha.etymology_analysis: Village of Raksha in Morshansky District, Tambov Oblast, founded in the mid-17th century CE and first documented in 1678 CE.

b_chatzk.first_mention_attestation: 1553 CE foundation of the Muscovite fortress of Shatsk (Shatsky gorod) on the Shacha River.
b_chatzk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Shacha River (a pre-Slavic Finno-Ugric hydronym); founded as a Russian defensive fortress in 1553 CE.

b_khortytsia.first_mention_attestation: 1103 CE Primary Chronicle (sub anno 6611 AM) mentioning the island of Khortitsa (earlier attested c. 950 CE by Constantine VII as St. George Island).

morphemes.translation: possibly Slavic deity Khors or Turkic khort

b_khortytsia.etymology_analysis: Dnieper island first attested as St. George Island c. 950 CE and as Khortitsa in 1103 CE (both post-867 CE); etymology is debated between the Slavic deity Khors and Turkic/Iranian roots.

b_mariupol.first_mention_attestation: 1779–1780 CE (Russian imperial founding of Mariupol on the site of the Cossack outpost Domakha for resettled Crimean Greeks)
b_mariupol.eponym_details: Named in honor of Grand Duchess Maria Feodorovna (1759–1828), wife of the future Tsar Paul I (with secondary association to the Virgin Mary).
b_mariupol.etymology_analysis: Greek-styled compound 'City of Maria', bestowed in 1779–1780 CE when Crimean Greeks were resettled to the former Zaporozhian Cossack fortress of Domakha at the mouth of the Kalmius River.

b_kutur-ogly.first_mention_attestation: Attested prior to 1827 CE as a Nogai Tatar aul (Kutur-Ogly) on the site of modern Berdyansk
b_kutur-ogly.eponym_details: Turkic/Nogai patronymic 'Kutur-Ogly' ('son of Kutur'), referring to a post-867 Nogai clan or founder.
b_kutur-ogly.etymology_analysis: Nogai Tatar settlement name meaning 'son of Kutur', attested in the early 19th century CE before the Russian port of Berdyansk was built there in 1827 CE.

b_donetsk.first_mention_attestation: 1961 CE (city renamed Donetsk; originally founded 1869 CE as Yuzovka on the site of Aleksandrovka, attested 1779 CE)
b_donetsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Seversky Donets River ('Little Don'); the city was founded in 1869 CE as Yuzovka (after Welsh industrialist John Hughes) and renamed Donetsk in 1961 CE.

b_oleshye.first_mention_attestation: 1084 CE in the Primary Chronicle (Povest Vremennykh Let) as Olshiya / Oleshia
b_oleshye.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic *ol'shye ('alder grove'), referring to the forested wetlands of the Lower Dnieper; first attested in the Primary Chronicle under 1084 CE as a Kievan Rus' port.

b_kakovka.first_mention_attestation: 1791 CE (founded as Kakhovka on the site of the 1492 CE Crimean Tatar fortress Islam-Kermen)
b_kakovka.eponym_details: Named after Russian governor Vasily Kakhovsky (1738–1795).
b_kakovka.etymology_analysis: Named in 1791 CE after Russian governor Vasily Kakhovsky; built on the site of the Crimean Tatar fortress Islam-Kermen (founded 1492 CE, also called Aslan-Gorod in Russian sources).

b_kyzyl_jar.first_mention_attestation: Late 18th to early 19th century CE (Nogai aul Kiz-Yar / Kyzyl-Yar, now the Kiziyar district of Melitopol)
b_kyzyl_jar.etymology_analysis: Turkic topographic name meaning 'red ravine' (or 'maiden's ravine' in local Nogai legend), referring to the Kiziyar gully in modern Melitopol, settled in the late 18th–19th century CE.

b_kozlov.first_mention_attestation: 1627 CE (monastery in the forest), followed by the 1635 CE frontier town of Kozlov on the Belgorod Line (renamed Michurinsk in 1932 CE)
b_kozlov.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive toponym derived from *kozel* ('goat') or a local pioneer/tract name Kozlov; founded as a monastery in 1627 CE and fortified town in 1635 CE.

b_oranienburg.first_mention_attestation: 1702 CE (fortress built by Peter the Great and named Oranienburg, later Ranenburg and Chaplygin)
b_oranienburg.eponym_details: Transferred in 1702 CE by Peter the Great from Oranienburg in Brandenburg, which itself was renamed in 1652 CE after Countess Louise Henriette of Nassau (1627–1667), Princess of Orange (House of Orange-Nassau).
b_oranienburg.etymology_analysis: Transferred in 1702 CE by Peter the Great from the German town of Oranienburg in Brandenburg; later Russianized to Ranenburg and renamed Chaplygin in 1948 CE.

b_saran.first_mention_attestation: 1641 CE (founded as Saransky ostrozhek / Saransk at the confluence of the Saranka and Insar rivers)
b_saran.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Saranka River (Mordvin *sara* 'sedge marsh'); the Russian frontier fort Saransky ostrozhek (modern Saransk) was founded in 1641 CE.

b_vorona.first_mention_attestation: 13th century CE (attested as the boundary river between the Sarai and Ryazan eparchies)
b_vorona.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Vorona River (tributary of the Khopyor), likely from a Finno-Ugric root *vor/*vur ('forest'), folk-etymologized in Russian as *vorona* ('crow').

b_kachma.first_mention_attestation: Post-medieval Russian hydrological records (Kashma River, tributary of the Tsna in Tambov Oblast; no pre-867 CE written attestation)
b_kachma.etymology_analysis: Substrate hydronym of the Kashma River (right tributary of the Tsna in Tambov Oblast), of pre-Russian Finno-Ugric origin, unattested in written sources before the Russian colonization of the Tsna basin.

b_serdosk.first_mention_attestation: 1698 CE (founded as Serdobskaya sloboda on the Serdoba River; granted town status as Serdobsk in 1780 CE)
b_serdosk.etymology_analysis: Russian town name formed with *-sk* from the Serdoba River; founded in 1698 CE as a frontier sloboda by Penza border guards.

b_kirsanov.first_mention_attestation: First half of the 17th century CE (founded as the settlement of Kirsanovo; town status 1779 CE)
b_kirsanov.eponym_details: Named after Kirsan Zubakin, the first 17th-century Russian settler in the area.
b_kirsanov.etymology_analysis: Possessive settlement name derived from the 17th-century pioneer Kirsan Zubakin; originally Kirsanovo, elevated to town status as Kirsanov in 1779 CE.

b_durovka.first_mention_attestation: 18th century CE (village of Durovka in Kozlov uyezd, Tambov Governorate, owned by landowner Maria Durova)
b_durovka.eponym_details: Named after landowner Maria Durova (or the Durov noble family) of Kozlov uyezd.
b_durovka.etymology_analysis: Russian estate village name derived from the landowner surname Durov (specifically Maria Durova in Kozlov uyezd, Tambov region).

b_kolychev.first_mention_attestation: Post-16th century CE Russian estate toponym (derived from the Muscovite boyar/noble surname Kolychev)
b_kolychev.eponym_details: Derived from the Russian noble surname Kolychev (attested from the 14th–15th century CE onward).
b_kolychev.etymology_analysis: Possessive settlement name from the Russian noble surname Kolychev, reflecting post-medieval Russian gentry landholding in the Tambov-Voronezh frontier.

b_repnoye.first_mention_attestation: Late 18th century CE (attested in the Economic Notes of Borisoglebsk Uyezd as 'newly settled village Repnaya')
b_repnoye.etymology_analysis: Russian agricultural toponym meaning 'turnip place', founded in the late 18th century CE in Uvarovsky District, Tambov Oblast.

b_matya.first_mention_attestation: Mid-17th century CE (Russian settlements along the Matyra River in Kozlov and Lipetsk uyezds)
b_matya.etymology_analysis: Shortened/variant form of the Matyra River hydronym (a major left tributary of the Voronezh River in Tambov and Lipetsk oblasts), of pre-Slavic substrate origin but unattested in writing prior to the 17th century CE.

b_plavitza.first_mention_attestation: Post-17th century CE Russian hydrological and settlement records (Plavitsa River, tributary of the Matyra)
b_plavitza.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Plavitsa River (left tributary of the Matyra), from Russian dialectal *plav* ('bog, quagmire'), giving its name to several 17th–19th century CE villages.

b_tambov.first_mention_attestation: 1636 CE (founded in spring 1636 CE as a Russian fortress on the Tsna River)
b_tambov.etymology_analysis: Derived from a pre-Russian Mordvin (Moksha/Erzya) word meaning 'the remote/other side' or 'swampy/deep pool' (referring to the Lesnoy Tambov river), adopted for the 1636 CE Russian fortress.

b_szava.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in 867 CE; corresponds to a regional Tambov-basin hydronym (Savala or Shacha, the latter first attested in 1627 CE)
b_szava.etymology_analysis: Game-adopted form in the Tambov region, likely reflecting the Savala River (tributary of the Khopyor) or the Shacha River (attested 1627 CE, from Mordvin *shachims* 'fertile').

b_kuzeytorg.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; modern game-constructed Turkic-Slavic hybrid name
b_kuzeytorg.etymology_analysis: Modern synthetic hybrid of Turkic *kuzey* ('north') and Slavic *torg* ('market'), created for the game's Lower Don / Azov region with no historical attestation.

b_ivanovskoye.first_mention_attestation: Post-18th century CE Russian settlement name in the Lower Don / Azov region (no pre-867 CE attestation)
b_ivanovskoye.etymology_analysis: Standard Russian possessive village name formed from the personal name Ivan (John), characteristic of 18th–19th century CE Russian/Cossack colonization along the Lower Don.

b_tana.first_mention_attestation: Early 14th century CE (Venetian and Genoese trading colony of La Tana at the mouth of the Don River)
b_tana.etymology_analysis: Medieval Italian (Venetian/Genoese) name for the 14th-century CE trading colony at modern Azov, derived from the ancient Greek name *Tanais* for the Don River and its delta city.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Bosporan Greek inscriptions, archaeological evidence (first quarter of the 3rd century BCE, c. 275 BCE), and Strabo's Geography.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek Tanais (excavated at Nedvigovka in the Don delta) served as the classical predecessor emporium to medieval Tana (Azov).

b_taganrog.first_mention_attestation: 1698 CE (founded by Peter the Great as Troitsky-on-Taganrog on Cape Tagany Rog)
b_taganrog.etymology_analysis: Compound of Turkic *tagan* ('tripod/brazier stand', referring to a beacon) and Russian *rog* ('cape/promontory'); founded as a Russian naval base in 1698 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus, Histories, Book IV (5th century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek emporion Kremnoi ('Cliffs'), probably situated at or near the Taganrog promontory.

b_karatayak.first_mention_attestation: 1647 CE (founded as the Russian fortress of Korotoyak / Karatayak on the Belgorod Line)
b_karatayak.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym (*kara-tau-yak*, 'black-mountain bank') for a small Don tributary and bluff, adapted into Russian as *Korotoyak* when the fortress was built in 1647 CE.

b_pavlovsk.first_mention_attestation: 1709 CE (founded by Peter the Great as Osered fortress and shipyard; renamed Pavlovsk in 1711–1715 CE)
b_pavlovsk.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1709 CE on the Osered River and renamed Pavlovsk in 1711–1715 CE after St. Paul's fortress (whose garrison was transferred there from the Mius).

b_babrov.first_mention_attestation: 1698 CE (established as Bobrovskaya Sloboda; granted town status as Bobrov in 1779 CE)
b_babrov.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name derived from *bobr* ('beaver'), founded in 1698 CE on the Bityug River as Bobrovskaya Sloboda and renamed Bobrov in 1779 CE.

b_khursa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; Alanic/Ossetian-styled game toponym in the Upper Don region
b_khursa.etymology_analysis: Unattested Alanic/Ossetian-inspired toponym (cf. Ossetian *xurs* 'sun') placed in the medieval Alanic-Slavic Saltovo-Mayaki zone of the Don basin.

b_khorysdan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; Alanic/Ossetian-styled game toponym in the Upper Don region
b_khorysdan.etymology_analysis: Unattested Alanic/Ossetian-inspired compound (cf. Ossetian *xorz* 'good' + *don* 'river') placed in the Don basin.

b_oskol.first_mention_attestation: 1185 CE in the Ipatiev Chronicle (as the gathering point Oskol for Princes Igor and Svyatoslav)
b_oskol.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Oskol River; first attested in the Ipatiev Chronicle under 1185 CE and refounded as a Russian fortress in 1593 CE (now Stary Oskol).

b_chally-kala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; Turkic-styled fortress name in the Oskol/Donets steppe
b_chally-kala.etymology_analysis: Turkic-styled fortress name ('Chally Fortress') without pre-867 CE historical attestation in the Oskol basin.

b_voronezh.first_mention_attestation: 1177 CE in East Slavic chronicles (Prince Yaropolk of Ryazan fleeing 'to Voronozh'); Russian fortress founded 1586 CE
b_voronezh.etymology_analysis: Named after the Voronezh River (probably from Slavic *voron* 'raven/black' or a Finno-Ugric substrate); first attested in chronicles under 1177 CE, with a modern fortress built in 1586 CE.

b_usman.first_mention_attestation: 1645 CE (founded as an ostrog on the Belgorod Line and named after the Usman River)
b_usman.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Usman River (likely of Iranian or Turkic substrate origin); the Russian fortress was founded in 1645 CE and granted town status in 1779 CE.

b_lipetsk.first_mention_attestation: 1284 CE (medieval settlement destroyed by the Mongols; modern town founded 1703 CE)
b_lipetsk.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic *lipa* ('linden tree'), meaning 'Linden town'; a medieval predecessor was destroyed in 1284 CE and the modern city was founded in 1703 CE.

b_dnipro.first_mention_attestation: 2016 CE (renamed Dnipro; earlier Yekaterinoslav 1787 CE and Dnipropetrovsk 1926 CE; Cossack settlement from 1524/1645 CE)
b_dnipro.etymology_analysis: Named after the Dnieper (Dnipro) River in 2016 CE; the modern city was founded as Yekaterinoslav in 1787 CE on the site of earlier 16th–17th century CE Cossack settlements.

b_salmacatce.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; appears to be a game-adapted or garbled medieval portolan/classical form
b_salmacatce.etymology_analysis: Unattested toponym placed in the Lower Dnieper (Dnipro) county in-game with no verified pre-867 CE attestation.

b_ladyzyn.first_mention_attestation: 1240 CE (attested as Ladyzhyn in the 13th century CE; burned in 1363 CE during Lithuanian-Tatar conflicts)
b_ladyzyn.etymology_analysis: East Slavic possessive settlement name on the Southern Bug, first documented in the 13th–14th centuries CE (1240/1363 CE).

b_birzula.first_mention_attestation: 1772 CE (first mentioned in Ottoman documents as Birzula in the Dubossar raya)
b_birzula.etymology_analysis: Romanian/Moldovan settlement name (Bârzula) first attested in Ottoman records in 1772 CE; renamed Kotovsk in 1935 CE and Podilsk in 2016 CE.

b_liubashivka.first_mention_attestation: 18th century CE (founded in southern Ukraine; railway station built 1868 CE)
b_liubashivka.etymology_analysis: Ukrainian settlement name formed with *-ivka* from the personal name Lyubash/Lyubasha, founded in the 18th century CE.

b_yary.first_mention_attestation: Modern Ukrainian settlement name (khutor Yary in Khrystynivka/Uman Raion; no pre-867 CE attestation)
b_yary.etymology_analysis: Ukrainian plural topographic term *yary* ('ravines, gullies', borrowed from Turkic *yar*), used for a small khutor in the Uman area.

b_buky.first_mention_attestation: Late 16th century CE (settlement known on the Hirskyi Tikych River in Cherkasy Oblast)
b_buky.etymology_analysis: Ukrainian plural noun *buky* ('beech trees'), referring to beech groves along the Hirskyi Tikych River; attested since the late 16th century CE.

b_uman.first_mention_attestation: 1616 CE (first mentioned in Polish-Lithuanian documents as a fortified town on the Umanka River)
b_uman.etymology_analysis: Named after the Umanka River; first attested in historical documents in 1616 CE as a Polish-Lithuanian border fort against Tatar raids.

b_atbasar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1845 CE as the Russian Cossack stanitsa Atbasarskaya on the Zhabay River; granted city status in 1878–1879 CE.
b_atbasar.etymology_analysis: Derived from Kazakh at ('horse') + bazar ('market'), referring to the site's early role as a steppe horse-trading fairground.

older_name_by_867.notes: No settlement or toponym at this site is attested in written sources on or before 867 CE.

b_chargaldzin.first_mention_attestation: Korgalzhyn (Russian: Kurgaldzhin) village was founded in 1928 CE as the center of Korgalzhyn District; the eponymous Lake Korgalzhyn appears in 19th-century CE Russian Imperial surveys.

morphemes.translation: marshy lake / steppe basin (exact Turkic root debated)

b_chargaldzin.etymology_analysis: Represents a historical/Russianized spelling (Chargaldzin / Kurgaldzhin) of Kazakh Qorğaljyn, the name of Lake Korgalzhyn and the surrounding depression in Akmola Region.

older_name_by_867.notes: No written attestation of Korgalzhyn/Chargaldzin exists on or before 867 CE.

b_jangyztau.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 19th-century CE Russian Imperial cartography as Zhalgyztau (Zhaksy-Zhalgyztau), a mountain and lake in northern Kazakhstan; no pre-19th-century CE written attestation is recorded.
b_jangyztau.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh jalğyz ('lone, solitary') + tau ('mountain'), referring to the isolated peak and adjacent lake Zhaksy-Zhalgyztau in North Kazakhstan / Akmola.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

b_burluk.first_mention_attestation: Nizhny Burluk was founded as a Russian Cossack stanitsa in 1849 CE; the Burluk (Imanburlyk/Akkanburlyk) river name is recorded in 19th-century CE Russian geographical surveys.
b_burluk.etymology_analysis: Turkic compound hydronym from bor/bur ('chalk/muddy sediment') + suffix -lyq/-luk, meaning 'muddy water / chalky sediment', applied to tributaries of the Ishim River.

older_name_by_867.notes: No written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_kafa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or geographical sources for northern Kazakhstan; appears only as a game-map barony name paired with Kokchetav (possibly a corruption of Lake Kopa at Kokshetau).
b_kafa.etymology_analysis: No verified local settlement or historical toponym 'Kafa' exists in the Kokshetau/Akmola region; likely a cartographic or game-data corruption (possibly of Kazakh Qopa, 'reed-filled lake', the lake beside Kokshetau).

older_name_by_867.notes: No historical settlement or pre-867 CE attestation.

b_kokchetav.first_mention_attestation: Founded in May 1824 CE as a Russian administrative and military outpost named Kokchetav (renamed Kokshetau in 1993 CE).
b_kokchetav.etymology_analysis: Russianized form (Kokchetav) of Kazakh Kökşetau ('bluish/smoky-blue mountain'), named after Mount Kokshe in the Kokshetau Uplands.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation for the settlement or mountain name.

b_kostanay.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Russian settlers in 1879 CE as Nikolaevsk (in honor of Tsar Nicholas II) and renamed Kustanay/Kostanay upon receiving city status in 1893–1895 CE.
b_kostanay.eponym_details: Folk etymology sometimes links the name to an 18th-century CE Kazakh warrior, batyr Kostan (Kostan Almambetuly), though scholarly sources treat Qostanay as a Turkic toponym.
b_kostanay.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Qostanai (Russianized as Kustanay until 1997 CE). Its exact root is debated between a compound with qos ('twin/pair') and a local personal/tribal name.

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded in 1879 CE as Nikolaevsk; no pre-867 CE settlement or name attested.

b_ore.first_mention_attestation: The Or River (Russian: Or', Kazakh: Or) is documented in Russian Imperial records from the founding of the Orsk/Orenburg fortress at its mouth in 1735 CE.
b_ore.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Turkic hydronym Or (Kazakh Or, Bashkir Ur/Ür, meaning 'ditch, trench, channel'), a left tributary of the Ural River rising in the Mugodzhar Hills.

older_name_by_867.notes: No written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_kurgan.first_mention_attestation: Settled between 1659 and 1662 CE as Tsaryovo Gorodishche by Timofey Nevezhin; renamed Kurgan upon receiving city status in 1782 CE.
b_kurgan.etymology_analysis: Named after a large ancient artificial burial mound (kurgan, from Turkic qorğan) located near the original 17th-century CE Russian frontier settlement of Tsaryovo Gorodishche.

older_name_by_867.notes: Earlier name Tsaryovo Gorodishche dates to 1659–1662 CE, well after 867 CE.

b_ukavskaya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern gazetteers of Kurgan Oblast; appears as a Russian-style adjectival (-skaya) barony name in the Kurgan region.
b_ukavskaya.etymology_analysis: Bears the Russian feminine adjectival suffix -skaya typical of 18th–19th-century CE Siberian/Trans-Ural settlements, though no verified historical settlement named Ukavskaya is documented.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE attestation.

b_baklansky.first_mention_attestation: Baklanskoye (Kargapolsky District, Kurgan Oblast) was founded around 1680 CE as the village of Baklanskaya (temporarily renamed Georgiyevskoye before reverting to Baklanskoye).
b_baklansky.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival settlement name derived from the Baklanka River (at its confluence with the Miass River), from Russian baklan ('cormorant').

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded around 1680 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_sabakyul.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-modern written attestation; represents a Turkic lake toponym in the Kurgan–Tobol steppe zone.
b_sabakyul.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym ending in kül/köl ('lake'), with the first element likely Turkic saba ('leather skin/vessel') or a dialectal fish/plant term.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE attestation.

b_tobol_bis.first_mention_attestation: The Tobol River is attested in Russian Siberian chronicles from the late 16th century CE (e.g., founding of Tobolsk in 1587 CE); the qualifier 'Bis' is a modern/game-map distinction.
b_tobol_bis.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Tobol River (Kazakh Tobyl, traditionally linked to Turkic tobulğu, 'meadowsweet') with the qualifier bis ('second' or 'five').

older_name_by_867.notes: No written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_abugan.first_mention_attestation: The Ubagan (historical Russian: Abugan/Abagana, Kazakh: Obağan) river is attested in 18th–19th-century CE Russian Imperial geographical works (e.g., Brockhaus and Efron Encyclopedic Dictionary).

morphemes.translation: river name (linked to oba 'mound' or Kazakh folklore 'Übbe', water spirit)

b_abugan.etymology_analysis: Variant of Kazakh Obağan (Russianized as Ubagan/Abugan), a 376-km right tributary of the Tobol flowing through Lake Kushmurun.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_skramlrak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical, geographical, or linguistic sources; appears to be a garbled or corrupted cartographic label in the Abugan/Kostanay region.
b_skramlrak.etymology_analysis: No verified historical or linguistic attestation; likely a transcription error or garbled map label.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE attestation.

b_karasu.first_mention_attestation: Karasu village in Kostanay Region became a district center when Karasu District was established in 1939 CE; the Karasu River hydronym is documented in 19th-century CE Russian surveys.
b_karasu.etymology_analysis: Common Turkic hydronym from qara ('black') + su ('water'), denoting slow-moving, dark, or spring-fed steppe streams.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kak.first_mention_attestation: Lake Kak (Kazakh: Qaq / Ülken Qaq) in North Kazakhstan Region is documented in modern Russian and Kazakh geographical surveys; no pre-867 CE attestation exists.

morphemes.translation: rainwater puddle, shallow steppe salt lake

b_kak.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh qaq ('shallow steppe basin/salt lake collecting meltwater'), referring to Lake Kak in North Kazakhstan.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kush-murun.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1830s–1840s CE (birthplace of Shoqan Walikhanov in 1835 CE at Aman-Karagai / Kushmurun fort; railway station founded 1939 CE).
b_kush-murun.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Qūsmūryn (Russianized Kushmurun), literally 'bird's beak' (or 'twin promontory'), referring to the elongated lake and its protruding peninsulas in Kostanay Region.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_auliekol.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1879 CE (or 1897 CE per Russian Wikipedia) on the site of a 19th-century CE Kazakh aul; known as Semiozernoye until renamed Auliekol in 1997 CE.
b_auliekol.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh äulie ('holy', borrowed from Arabic awliyāʾ) + köl ('lake'), meaning 'Holy Lake', named after the nearby Lake Auliekol.

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded in the late 19th century CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_kamichly_kul.first_mention_attestation: No pre-modern written attestation; Turkic hydronym ('reedy lake') attested in 19th–20th-century CE Russian Imperial/Soviet maps of the Turgay/Kostanay steppe.
b_kamichly_kul.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym from qamyşly ('reedy', from qamyş 'reed') + kül/köl ('lake'), meaning 'reedy lake'.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_jitikul.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1880 CE as the Kazakh settlement Konildi on the Shortandy River; later known as Dzhetygara (renamed Zhitikara in 1997 CE).
b_jitikul.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh jeti ('seven') + köl ('lake') or qara ('black'), rendered in Russian/German cartography as Jitikul / Dschetiköl / Dzhetygara (modern Zhitikara).

older_name_by_867.notes: First mentioned in 1880 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_dantenkul.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-modern written attestation; appears as a Turkic lake name (-kul/-köl) in the Kostanay/Jitikul region.
b_dantenkul.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym containing the element kul/köl ('lake') with an obscure first element Danten-.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE attestation.

b_kos_uba.first_mention_attestation: Documented in 19th–20th-century CE Russian Imperial and Kazakh geographical records as Kosoba/Kos-Uba ('twin mounds').
b_kos_uba.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh qos ('pair, twin') + oba ('mound, hill'), a common steppe toponym referring to twin hills or mounds.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_airyk.first_mention_attestation: Mount Airyk in the Mugodzhar Mountains and settlements named Airyk in Aktobe Region are documented in modern Russian and Kazakh geographical surveys.
b_airyk.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh airyq ('fork, branching valley, mountain pass'), naming Mount Airyk in the Mugodzhar Hills and nearby localities in Aktobe Region.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kos_biryuk.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-modern written attestation; Kazakh steppe toponym in the Mugodzhar region.
b_kos_biryuk.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh compound with qos ('pair, twin') and biryuk/börük (possibly 'wolf' or a Russianized form of a Kazakh stem).

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kosh_kurbay.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-modern written attestation; appears in the Mugodzhar Hills region (likely Kazakh Qoshqarbai).
b_kosh_kurbay.etymology_analysis: Likely a transcription of Kazakh Qoshqarbai (qoshqar 'ram' + bai 'rich/noble'), a traditional Kazakh personal or clan-associated toponym.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_jarli_butak.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-modern written attestation; Kazakh hydronym in the Mugodzhar/Or basin.
b_jarli_butak.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh jarly ('having steep banks/cliffs') + būtaq ('branch, tributary stream'), a descriptive hydronym in western Kazakhstan.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_karabutak.first_mention_attestation: Fort Karabutak was founded on May 13–14, 1848 CE by Russian troops on the Karabutak River (tributary of the Irgiz); visited and sketched by Taras Shevchenko in 1848–1850 CE.
b_karabutak.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Qarabūtaq (qara 'black' + būtaq 'branch/tributary'), named after the Karabutak River in Aktobe Region.

older_name_by_867.notes: Fort founded in 1848 CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kum_sai.first_mention_attestation: Kumsai (Kum-Sai) in Aktobe Region is attested in early 20th-century CE Russian Imperial/ornithological records (e.g., Karamzin 1917 CE, 'Kum-Sai, Aktyubinsk district, Turgai province').
b_kum_sai.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Qūmsai (qūm 'sand' + sai 'ravine/gully'), literally 'sandy ravine'.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_chir_kala.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-modern written attestation for a site named Chir Kala in the Mugodzhar Hills region.
b_chir_kala.etymology_analysis: Contains the Turkic/Arabic element qala ('fortress, town') preceded by an uncertain modifier chir/sher.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_jity_kul.first_mention_attestation: Lake Zhetikol (Russian: Zhetykol) in the Orenburg–Aktobe steppe is documented in modern Russian and Kazakh geographical registries; no pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_jity_kul.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Jeti-köl (jeti 'seven' + köl 'lake'), meaning 'Seven Lakes'.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_petropavl.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1752 CE as the Russian military Fortress of Saint Peter (St. Peter and St. Paul) on the Ishim River; granted city status as Petropavlovsk in 1807 CE.
b_petropavl.eponym_details: Named after the Christian apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul (1st century CE), following the 1752 CE Russian Fortress of Saint Peter.
b_petropavl.etymology_analysis: Kazakh form Petropavl of Russian Petropavlovsk, named after Saints Peter and Paul from the 1752 CE Russian fortress; locally also known in Kazakh as Qyzyljar ('red cliff').

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded in 1752 CE; Kazakh name Qyzyljar is not attested on or before 867 CE.

b_uktuz.first_mention_attestation: Uktuz (originally the village of Uktuskaya/Uktuzskoye) in Berdyuzhsky District, Tyumen Oblast, was founded in 1771 CE.
b_uktuz.etymology_analysis: Russian village name derived from the nearby Uktuz lakes, incorporating Turkic tuz ('salt') with an uncertain first element uk-/aq-.

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded in 1771 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_mamlyutka.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1786 CE by Mavlyut (son of Vagiz) from Tyumen Okrug with his three sons; later grew around Mamlyutka railway station.
b_mamlyutka.eponym_details: Named after Mavlyut (son of Vagiz), a settler from Tyumen Okrug who founded the settlement in 1786 CE.
b_mamlyutka.etymology_analysis: Derived from the personal name of its 1786 CE founder, Mavlyut, adapted in Russian with the suffix -ka as Mamlyutka (Kazakh: Mämlüt).

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded in 1786 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_vargashi.first_mention_attestation: Vargashi settlement arose around Vargashi railway station opened on the Trans-Siberian Railway in 1896 CE, named after the nearby older village of Vargashi.
b_vargashi.etymology_analysis: Named after the nearby Trans-Ural village of Vargashi when the Trans-Siberian Railway station opened in 1896 CE.

older_name_by_867.notes: No pre-867 CE attestation.

b_mostovskoye.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1670 CE in the Trans-Ural region; known as Marayskoye until 1958 CE, when it was renamed Mostovskoye.
b_mostovskoye.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival name from most ('bridge') + -ovskoye, adopted in 1958 CE in place of its earlier name Marayskoye.

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded around 1670 CE as Marayskoye; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_shchuchye.first_mention_attestation: Known since 1750 CE as a Russian selo on Lake Shchuchye; granted town status in 1945 CE.
b_shchuchye.etymology_analysis: Russian hydronymic settlement name from shchuka ('pike'), meaning 'Pike [Lake]', after adjacent Lake Shchuchye.

older_name_by_867.notes: Known since 1750 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_astrakhan.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as Hajji Tarkhan by Ibn Battuta in 1333 CE (modern Astrakhan established in 1558 CE).
b_astrakhan.eponym_details: According to a Tatar legend recorded by Ibn Battuta, Hajji Tarkhan was named after a Turkic pilgrim (hajji) granted tax-exempt (tarkhan) status.
b_astrakhan.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of Golden Horde Hajji Tarkhan (attested 1333 CE by Ibn Battuta), located 12 km from modern Astrakhan (founded 1558 CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ibn Khordadbeh (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, mid-9th century CE, c. 846–885 CE) and Ibn Rusta; 10th-century CE sources (al-Istakhri, al-Mas'udi, Ibn Hawqal) later call the twin-city capital Atil / Khazaran.
older_name_by_867.notes: Khamlij (Hamlikh) is the 9th-century CE Arabic attestation for the Khazar Volga Delta capital near modern Astrakhan (later known as Atil / Khazaran in 10th-century CE sources).

b_sara.first_mention_attestation: If representing Sarai (Sarai Batu) on the Lower Volga, founded by Batu Khan in the mid-1240s CE; no pre-867 CE attestation of 'Sara' exists.
b_sara.etymology_analysis: Shortened or variant form of Sarai (from Persian sarāy 'palace, court'), the 13th-century CE Golden Horde capital on the Akhtuba/Lower Volga; unattested on or before 867 CE.

b_khazaran.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century CE classical Arabic geographical sources (al-Istakhri, al-Mas'udi, and Ibn Hawqal, c. 930–950 CE) and the Schechter Letter as the commercial half of the Khazar Volga capital; 9th-century CE sources (Ibn Khordadbeh) refer to the Khazar capital as Khamlij / Hamlikh.
b_khazaran.etymology_analysis: Persian/Arabic plural-locative formation Khazaran ('[city of] the Khazars'), denoting the commercial half of the Khazar capital Atil in the Volga Delta.

b_beksima.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation documented; unattested Lower Volga steppe toponym.
b_beksima.etymology_analysis: Likely a Turkic compound incorporating bek ('lord, chieftain'), used for a Lower Volga holding; no historical attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_sarepta.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1765 CE by Moravian Brethren (Volga German) colonists south of Tsaritsyn.

morphemes.translation: biblical town, adapted to the nearby Sarpa River

b_sarepta.etymology_analysis: Named in 1765 CE by Moravian Brethren settlers after biblical Sarepta (1 Kings 17:9–10), echoing the nearby Sarpa River.

b_yenotayevka.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1742 CE as a Russian fortress (the nearby Yenotayevskaya hill was first recorded in 1703 CE by Cornelis de Bruijn).

morphemes.translation: side of the mountain (yan + tau) or personal name

b_yenotayevka.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement suffix -evka attached to Yenotai (either from Turkic yan 'side' + tau 'mountain', referring to the high Volga bank, or a local personal name); founded in 1742 CE.

b_sarkel.first_mention_attestation: Built by the Khazars with Byzantine engineering assistance in the 830s CE (c. 834–838 CE), attested in Byzantine chronicles (Theophanes Continuatus, De Administrando Imperio).
b_sarkel.etymology_analysis: Khazar (Oghur Turkic) Šarkel ('white house/fortress'), referring to its white limestone-and-brick walls built in the 830s CE; later translated into East Slavic as Belaya Vezha.

b_aksay.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1569 CE as a Don Cossack settlement (Ust-Aksayskaya).
b_aksay.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym Aqsai ('white/clear gully or stream', from aq 'white' + sai 'ravine/stream'); the Cossack settlement is first recorded in 1569 CE.

b_semikarakary.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1672 CE as the Don Cossack stanitsa of Semikarakorskaya.

morphemes.translation: black hill/ridge or 'seven black fortresses' (folk etymology)

b_semikarakary.etymology_analysis: Russian-Turkic compound (semi- 'seven' + Turkic qara 'black' / qor 'fortification' or personal/clan name); the Cossack stanitsa is known from 1672 CE, near an unnamed 8th–9th century CE Khazar fortress.

older_name_by_867.notes: An unnamed late 8th–early 9th century CE Khazar brick fortress (Semikarakorsk Fortress) lies nearby, but its contemporary pre-867 CE name is unattested.
